So much for the super-dry El Nino eh! It is raining whilst writing this report and there is plenty more on the way apparently. The weather is rather unappealing for boaties and landlubbers alike at present. Today's 15-20 knot north-easter is supposedly going to ease a tad tomorrow, but not by much. Expect at least 15 knots at times Saturday and more like 15-20 knots Sunday after the breeze tends more northerly. Showers, rain and the chance of storms all adding to a very gloomy weekend outlook. The working week won't kick off much better either. Storms could roll in from out west, whilst showers blown onshore remain likely. The wind will still be quite stiff initially, from the north to north-west through Monday, before finally easing below 15 knots Tuesday. Who knows what the future thereafter might bring. It is indeed a stretch to forecast even a day or two ahead nowadays. So, batten down the hatches and settle in for a rather damp few days. As pleasant and comfortable as our climate feels right now, it is hard to visualise any joy for boaties beyond sheltered waters for a few days to come. Today's 15 knot easterly is set to strengthen slightly during Saturday and restrict boaties all weekend. Winds are likely to kick-off each day at 15 knots then build to 20 if not 25 knots. Saturday looks the worst, with a subtle improvement possible Sunday. The chance of showers is increasing day by day too. Not enough to soak our parched landscape, but welcome all the same if we can get a few mm per day. Gradually improving weather into the next working week will open up opportunities for frustrated boaties. The high-pressure system that has stalled in the Tasman Sea will hopefully weaken enough to see winds lighten. Offshore will still be limited to larger vessels, but the eastern and southern bay should be okay. The moon is waxing again after the passing of the new moon phase last Sunday. reports.text: Wet and windy conditions are expected this weekend, so anglers will be best served heading up the creeks to escape the worst of the showers and south-easterly winds. With the overcast conditions, mangrove jacks should be high on the target list. Surface lures such as frogs and 70-90mm poppers worked tight against snaggy structure are worth a look, while live baits and fresh strips of mullet continue to produce fish. Even when the jacks are quiet, there are usually plenty of cod and bream around to keep rods bending. A few stocked Tin Can Bay barramundi have also been caught over the past couple of weeks as water temperatures continue to rise. Live baits have accounted for some captures, while slowly worked soft plastic prawns remain a reliable option. Crabbing has been a little quiet, although the recent rainfall should help get the crabs moving. It’s still worth setting a few pots, with fresh baits and a longer soak generally producing the best results.

reports.text: Mackerel remain the headline act across the region, with broadbar and school mackerel dominating catches around the Urangan Pier, local beaches and the wider bay. The pier is also producing quality queenfish, giant trevally, golden trevally and the occasional Spanish mackerel, while whiting continue to be caught along the Hervey Bay foreshores and throughout the Great Sandy Straits. The Great Sandy Straits and local river systems are fishing well for grunter, flathead, threadfin salmon, blue salmon and barramundi. Mangrove jacks are firing throughout the western creeks and the Burrum system, while quality whiting are also featuring in the middle reaches. Offshore, coral trout, grassy sweetlip, cod and Spanish mackerel continue to feature, while billfish activity is building with juvenile black marlin, striped marlin and yellowfin tuna all being reported. Around Rooneys Point and Station Hill, the first consistent run of juvenile black marlin for the season has provided plenty of excitement for gamefishers. Fraser Island’s tailor season remains patchy depending on location and conditions, although quality greenbacks are still being caught through the central sector. Anglers are also finding dart, whiting and the occasional trevally along the surf beaches. Boaties should remain aware of lingering whale traffic and patches of nuisance “snot weed” in parts of Platypus Bay and the central bay.
reports.credit: Coastwatch (Tin Can Bay section by The Chandlery Bait & Tackle)

reports.text: There are still some quality flathead being caught through the lower reaches of the Noosa River, with a number of better fish coming from the deeper channels and drop-offs. Bream and whiting remain the bread-and-butter species throughout the system, providing consistent fishing for both bait and lure anglers. A few tailor have also been taken by land-based anglers in the Noosaville reaches over the past week. Not a huge amount to report over the last week.  The closer offshore reefs were fishing well, with North Reef producing a reliable mix of snapper and sweetlip while further afield, Sunshine Reef was yielding quality pearl perch, while Double Island Point produced hard-fighting amberjack along with plenty of snapper. Plenty of fish being caught with The Hards, Double Island Point and North Reef all producing quality catches. A wide range of reef species are on the chew, making this one of the most productive times of the year to head offshore. With conditions and water temperatures aligning, both this month and next are shaping up as prime months for reef fishing, with anglers finding quality fish across both the close and wider grounds. The lower estuary continues to produce some quality flathead, while a number of belter bream have also been reported throughout the system. A few smaller mulloway are being caught in the ski run areas, with soft plastic frog-style lures proving effective on the jewies.

Further afield, reports of school and spotted mackerel have come from around Big Mick and Inskip Point. Traditional trolling methods such as planers rigged with small spoons are working, while small hardbodies in the 80-120mm range are also worth a try.

reports.text: Choosing the Right Bait for Fishing Around Rainbow Beach. The right bait around Rainbow Beach depends on where you fish and what you are chasing. Beach worms and pilchards work well for whiting and tailor off the surf, while live prawns and yabbies suit bream and flathead in the estuaries. Gardiner's Tackle World Rainbow Beach , a trusted bait fishing store in the region, stocks fresh and frozen bait for every trip, from the surf to Fraser Island and Double Island Point. Picking the correct bait can make or break a day on the water. Rainbow Beach offers such a wide variety of fishing grounds that a single bait choice rarely covers everything you might encounter. From the open surf beaches to the sheltered creeks of the Cooloola region, each spot calls for a different approach. That's why local anglers rely on a proper bait fishing store rather than guessing at the servo.
